sections.title: 1. Who is the audience and what do they need

keyTerms.definition: The people who will read or hear your work; each needs a different answer.
Write for the reader's expectations, not your own.

recall.question: What is the first move?
recall.answer: Name the audience and what they need; communication starts with the reader, not you.

keyTerms.definition: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion; each answers one question.
A paper is an argument your claim is true and new, dressed as a report.

recall.question: How do readers actually read?
recall.answer: Abstract, skim figures, decide whether to trust you; not front to back.

keyTerms.definition: A 20-minute talk can land one idea.
Hook, journey through tries including failures, result, takeaway.

recall.question: Why is a talk not a paper read aloud?
recall.answer: The audience cannot rewind or skip ahead, and remembers one thing the next day.

keyTerms.definition: A stranger gets the point in 30 seconds without reading the paper.
One of five figure rules; with axes, one message, uncertainty.

recall.question: What are the five figure rules?
recall.answer: Title states the message, axes carry meaning and units, one message per figure, annotate the point, show uncertainty.

keyTerms.definition: For ownership stories.
For research stories.
First; six mechanical rules for clear writing.

recall.question: What are the six writing rules?
recall.answer: Topic sentence first, short sentences, active voice, verbs carry action, define terms at first use, revise in passes.

sections.title: 6. The research communication: what it actually measures

keyTerms.definition: What the research-communication interview actually measures.
Projects, failures, conflicts, decisions; the right side.

recall.question: What do your papers prove versus your talk?
recall.answer: Papers prove you can do the work; talking proves you can do it with other people.

sections.title: 7. Your research narrative: the two-minute pitch

keyTerms.definition: Your work compressed into two minutes.
Draft, review, revise, repeat.

recall.question: What is the unsolved problem here?
recall.answer: Compressing your work into two minutes.

sections.title: 8. Failure stories: honesty as a signal

keyTerms.definition: Real mistake, real consequences, real changed behavior; the highest-signal 3 minutes.
Where the 3 minutes pay off.

recall.question: Why are failure stories credible?
recall.answer: Honesty about failure is hard; those who tell them well are instantly credible.

keyTerms.definition: Hold a technical position, listen, converge without burning the relationship.
Without burning the relationship.

recall.question: What are reviewers looking for?
recall.answer: Evidence you can fight well, not drama.

keyTerms.definition: About twenty separate knowing the framework from performing under pressure.
Anatomy check on paper fixes structural failure.
Partner follow-ups fix what breaks under questioning.

recall.question: What is the training plan?
recall.answer: Written, timed, recorded, drilled; each fixes a different failure.

sections.title: 11. Calibration: contrast and the senior bar

keyTerms.definition: Knowing where the bar is and where you stand relative to it.
Strong versus weak answers side by side.

recall.question: How does miscalibration run both ways?
recall.answer: Weak communicators think they did well (no contrast); strong ones think badly (impostor contrast).

keyTerms.definition: On writing and talks; state the problem up front.
Four talks from teachers famous for it.

recall.answer: Mountains versus molehills; seven concrete suggestions for writing, specific-to-general for talks.
